subject: Chemistry
q: On what basis are elements arranged in the modern periodic table?
explanation: Henry Moseley showed in 1913 that atomic number (the number of protons) is the fundamental property. Arranging by atomic number removed the anomalies of Mendeleev’s mass-based table, such as argon (39.9) coming before potassium (39.1).
misconception: Mendeleev used atomic mass; the modern table uses atomic number.
hints: It is the number of protons.

subject: Chemistry
q: Why does atomic radius increase down a group (for example from lithium to caesium)?
options: Nuclear charge decreases down a group.
Each element down the group has an extra electron shell.
Electrons become heavier down a group.
Atoms lose protons down a group.
explanation: Going down a group adds a whole new shell each time, so the outer electrons are much further from the nucleus. Nuclear charge does increase, but inner shells shield the outer electrons, so the extra shell dominates.
misconception: Nuclear charge increases down a group, but the added shell outweighs it.
hints: What changes about the number of shells down a group?

subject: Chemistry
q: How does metallic character change across Period 3 (from sodium to chlorine)?
options: It decreases, because atoms hold their outer electrons more tightly and tend to gain rather than lose electrons
explanation: Metals lose electrons easily. Across a period the nuclear charge grows and the atoms shrink, so the outer electrons are held more strongly. Elements change from reactive metals (Na, Mg) through a metalloid (Si) to non-metals (P, S, Cl).
hints: What makes an element metallic — losing or gaining electrons?

subject: Chemistry
q:
An element X has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 7. Consider:
I. X is in Group 17 and Period 3.
II. X forms the ion X⁻.
III. X is a metal.
IV. X combines with sodium to form an ionic compound NaX.
Which are correct?
explanation: Three shells → Period 3; seven valence electrons → Group 17 (halogens). It gains one electron to complete its octet, forming X⁻ — typical of a non-metal (III false). Sodium gives one electron to X, forming the ionic compound NaX. X is chlorine.
misconception: Seven valence electrons means gaining one, not losing seven.
hints: Shells give the period; valence electrons give the group.
Is it easier for X to gain 1 or lose 7 electrons?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why are noble gases such as neon and argon chemically very unreactive?
options: They are too heavy to react.
Their outermost shells are completely filled.
explanation: Neon (2, 8) and argon (2, 8, 8) have stable, full outer shells, so they have almost no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons. Other elements react to reach this kind of stable configuration.
hints: Write the electronic configuration of neon.

subject: Chemistry
q: In Döbereiner’s triad lithium (7), sodium (?), potassium (39), the middle element’s atomic mass is roughly the average of the other two. What value does this predict for sodium?
explanation: (7 + 39)/2 = 23, which matches sodium’s actual atomic mass (≈ 23). Döbereiner’s triads (1829) were an early hint of periodicity, but only a few such triads existed.
hints: Take the average of 7 and 39.

subject: Chemistry
q: What was the main limitation of Newlands’ Law of Octaves?
options: It included the noble gases incorrectly.
It placed elements by atomic number.
It worked only up to calcium; heavier elements did not fit the pattern of every eighth element being similar.
explanation: Newlands noticed that every eighth element (by atomic mass) had similar properties, like notes in music. The pattern broke down after calcium, and he forced some unlike elements together (e.g. iron with oxygen and sulphur). Noble gases had not yet been discovered.
hints: Did the pattern hold for heavy elements?

subject: Chemistry
q: An element X forms an oxide with the formula X₂O₃. What is the most likely formula of its chloride?
explanation: In X₂O₃, two X atoms balance three oxygens of valency 2: 2 × v = 3 × 2, so the valency of X is 3. Chlorine has valency 1, so the chloride is XCl₃ (for example aluminium: Al₂O₃ and AlCl₃).
misconception: X₂Cl₃ copies the oxide’s subscripts instead of working out the valency.
hints: Work out the valency of X from the oxide.
Chlorine’s valency is 1.

subject: Chemistry
q: How many periods (horizontal rows) and groups (vertical columns) does the modern periodic table have?
explanation: The long-form periodic table has 7 periods and 18 groups. The period number equals the number of electron shells being filled.
hints: Periods are rows; groups are columns.

subject: Chemistry
q: Which reacts most vigorously with water: lithium, sodium or potassium?
options: Potassium, because its outer electron is furthest from the nucleus and most easily lost
Lithium, because it is the smallest
Sodium, because it is in the middle
explanation: Reactivity of Group 1 metals increases down the group. Potassium’s single outer electron is in the fourth shell, well shielded and far from the nucleus, so it is lost most easily. Potassium reacts so violently that the hydrogen released catches fire with a lilac flame.
hints: How easily is each atom’s outer electron removed?

subject: Chemistry
q: Unlike Group 1 metals, the reactivity of the halogens (Group 17) DECREASES down the group. Why?
options: Halogens react by gaining an electron; in larger atoms the incoming electron is further from the nucleus and attracted less strongly.
Heavier halogens have fewer valence electrons.
The nuclear charge decreases down the group.
Halogens react by losing electrons, which is harder in bigger atoms.
explanation: Halogens need one electron to complete their outer shell. Fluorine is small, so an incoming electron is held very strongly — it is the most reactive non-metal. Down the group atoms get bigger and more shielded, so they attract an extra electron less strongly and reactivity falls (F > Cl > Br > I).
misconception: The trend reverses compared with Group 1 because halogens gain rather than lose electrons.
hints: Do halogens react by gaining or losing electrons?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why is the position of hydrogen in the periodic table considered unusual?
options: It resembles alkali metals (one valence electron, forms H⁺) and also halogens (needs one electron, forms H⁻ and H₂ molecules).
explanation: Hydrogen (configuration 1) has one electron like Group 1 metals and can form H⁺, but it is a diatomic non-metal gas that can also gain an electron to form H⁻ (as in NaH), like the halogens. So it does not fit neatly into either group.
hints: Compare hydrogen with both sodium and chlorine.

subject: Chemistry
q: Which of these is a chemical change?
explanation: Rusting forms a new substance (hydrated iron(III) oxide) with different properties and cannot easily be reversed. Melting, dissolving and breaking change only the state, arrangement or shape — physical changes.
hints: Which forms a new substance?

subject: Chemistry
q: Water is added to quicklime (calcium oxide). The mixture becomes very hot and forms slaked lime. Which statement describes this reaction?
options: A decomposition reaction that is endothermic
A combination reaction that is exothermic
explanation: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + heat. Two substances combine into one, and heat is released (exothermic). Slaked lime is used for whitewashing; it slowly reacts with CO₂ in air to form a shiny layer of calcium carbonate.
hints: How many products are formed, and does it get hot or cold?

subject: Chemistry
q: Water is electrolysed using inert electrodes. The gases collected at the two electrodes are in what volume ratio, hydrogen : oxygen?
explanation: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Two molecules of hydrogen form for each molecule of oxygen, and equal numbers of gas molecules occupy equal volumes, so the volume ratio is 2 : 1. (1 : 8 is the MASS ratio of hydrogen to oxygen in water.)
misconception: 1 : 8 is the mass ratio, not the volume ratio.
hints: Look at the coefficients in the balanced equation.

subject: Chemistry
q: During the electrolysis of acidified water, 20 mL of hydrogen is collected at the cathode. What volume of oxygen is collected at the anode at the same temperature and pressure?
explanation: The equation 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ gives hydrogen and oxygen in a 2 : 1 ratio by volume, so 20 mL of hydrogen comes with 10 mL of oxygen. 160 mL would be using the 1 : 8 mass ratio, which does not apply to volumes.
misconception: 160 mL wrongly applies the mass ratio to gas volumes.
hints: What is the mole (volume) ratio of H₂ to O₂ in the equation?
Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules.

subject: Chemistry
q: Sodium sulphate solution is mixed with barium chloride solution and a white solid immediately forms. What is the white solid?
explanation: Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄↓ + 2NaCl. The ions swap partners (double displacement). Barium sulphate is insoluble and forms a white precipitate, while sodium chloride stays dissolved. This is the standard test for sulphate ions.
misconception: Sodium chloride forms too, but it is soluble and stays in solution.
hints: The ions swap partners. Which product is insoluble?

subject: Chemistry
q: Propane (C₃H₈), the main fuel in some LPG, burns completely in oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water. In the balanced equation, how many molecules of O₂ are needed per molecule of propane?
explanation: C₃H₈ + ?O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O (balance C first, then H). Oxygen atoms on the right: 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 10, so 5 O₂ molecules are needed: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
misconception: 10 counts oxygen ATOMS; each O₂ molecule supplies two.
hints: Balance carbon, then hydrogen, then count oxygen atoms on the right.

subject: Chemistry
q: When ammonium chloride is dissolved in water in a test tube, the tube feels cold. What does this show?
options: The process is endothermic — it absorbs heat from the surroundings.
Ammonium chloride was stored in a refrigerator.
explanation: Dissolving ammonium chloride takes in more energy than it releases, so it draws heat from the water and the tube, lowering the temperature. Instant cold packs use similar endothermic dissolving.
hints: If something feels cold, where is the heat going?

subject: Chemistry
q: Equal masses of marble chips and powdered marble are added to separate flasks of the same dilute hydrochloric acid. The powder fizzes much more vigorously. What is the reason?
options: The acid is more concentrated in the second flask.
Powdered marble is a different chemical.
Powder has a much larger surface area, so more acid particles collide with it each second.
explanation: Reactions happen when particles collide. Grinding the marble exposes far more surface to the acid, increasing the rate of collisions and therefore the rate of CO₂ production. The total CO₂ eventually produced is the same, because the masses are equal.
misconception: The final amount of gas is the same; only the rate differs.
hints: Where do the acid and marble particles meet?
What does grinding do to the area of contact?

subject: Chemistry
q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes very slowly at room temperature, but bubbles rapidly when a pinch of manganese dioxide is added. Afterwards the manganese dioxide is recovered unchanged in mass. What is its role?
explanation: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. Manganese dioxide speeds up the reaction by providing an easier pathway, but is not used up — so it is a catalyst. Enzymes are biological catalysts.
hints: Was it used up in the reaction?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why does food keep longer in a refrigerator?
options: Lower temperature slows down the chemical reactions and microbial growth that spoil food.
explanation: Reaction rates — including those of enzymes in food and in microbes — fall sharply as temperature drops, because particles move more slowly and collide less often with enough energy. Refrigeration slows spoilage; it does not stop it entirely.
misconception: Most bacteria are not killed by refrigeration; their growth is slowed.
hints: How does temperature affect the rate of reactions?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which observation is NOT, on its own, evidence of a chemical reaction?
options: A precipitate appearing when two solutions mix
Bubbles of a new gas forming
explanation: Gas evolution, a precipitate, a permanent colour change or a temperature change can indicate that new substances are forming. A change in shape (bending wire, cutting paper) is a physical change.
hints: Which change produces no new substance?

subject: Chemistry
q: In a blast furnace, iron is produced by the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Which substance acts as the reducing agent?
explanation: Fe₂O₃ loses oxygen (it is reduced to Fe). CO gains oxygen (it is oxidised to CO₂). The substance that causes reduction and is itself oxidised is the reducing agent: carbon monoxide.
misconception: The substance that is reduced (Fe₂O₃) is the oxidising agent, not the reducing agent.
hints: Which reactant gains oxygen?

subject: Chemistry
q: What colour change does an acid produce with blue litmus paper?
explanation: Acids turn blue litmus red; bases turn red litmus blue. Neutral solutions leave both unchanged.
hints: Acids: blue → ?

subject: Chemistry
q: Zinc granules are added to dilute sulphuric acid and a gas bubbles off. A burning splint held at the mouth of the test tube goes out with a “pop”. What is the gas?
explanation: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Reactive metals displace hydrogen from dilute acids. Hydrogen burns explosively with oxygen in the air, giving the characteristic pop. Oxygen would relight a glowing splint; CO₂ would put the flame out silently.
hints: Metal + acid → salt + ?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why must concentrated acid always be added slowly to water, and never water to the acid?
options: The acid becomes stronger when water is added.
Dilution releases a lot of heat; adding water to acid can boil the water instantly and spray acid out.
Water reacts with acid to make a poisonous gas.
It does not matter which way round.
explanation: Dissolving a concentrated acid such as sulphuric acid in water is highly exothermic. If a little water is poured into a lot of acid, the water can boil locally and splash hot acid. Adding acid slowly to plenty of water spreads the heat safely.
hints: Is dilution of a concentrated acid exothermic or endothermic?

subject: Chemistry
q: In a titration, 25 mL of sodium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 50 mL of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.1 mol/L. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide? (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O)
explanation: Moles of HCl = 0.050 L × 0.1 mol/L = 0.005 mol. The reaction is 1 : 1, so NaOH = 0.005 mol in 0.025 L: concentration = 0.005/0.025 = 0.2 mol/L. It took twice the volume of acid, so the alkali must be twice as concentrated.
misconception: 0.05 mol/L inverts the volume ratio.
hints: Calculate moles of HCl used.
Moles of NaOH equal moles of HCl for a 1 : 1 reaction.

subject: Chemistry
q: Tooth enamel starts to dissolve when the pH in the mouth falls below about 5.5. Why does brushing with toothpaste help prevent decay?
options: Toothpaste is slightly basic and neutralises acids produced by bacteria feeding on sugar.
Toothpaste adds sugar for the teeth.
Toothpaste is acidic and kills bacteria.
explanation: Bacteria in plaque break down sugars and produce acids, lowering pH near the teeth. Enamel (calcium hydroxyapatite) dissolves in acid. Toothpastes are generally mildly basic, neutralising excess acid, and fluoride strengthens enamel.
hints: What produces acid in the mouth after eating sweets?

subject: Chemistry
q: A farmer finds that his soil is too acidic for his crop. What should he add?
options: More nitrogen fertiliser such as ammonium sulphate
explanation: Lime (calcium oxide or hydroxide) and chalk are bases that neutralise excess acid, raising soil pH. Vinegar and lemon juice are acidic, and ammonium fertilisers tend to make soil more acidic.
hints: What neutralises acids?

subject: Chemistry
q: Dry hydrogen chloride gas does not change the colour of DRY blue litmus paper, but it turns MOIST blue litmus paper red. What does this show?
options: The dry litmus paper was faulty.
HCl is a base when dry.
Acidic properties appear only when the acid forms H⁺ (H₃O⁺) ions, which requires water.
explanation: HCl molecules do not release hydrogen ions on their own. In water they ionise: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, and it is these ions that change the indicator. Acids show their acidic behaviour only in aqueous solution.
misconception: Pure water is neutral — the colour change comes from ions formed when HCl dissolves.
hints: What has to happen to HCl molecules before they behave as an acid?
What does the water in the moist paper allow?

subject: Chemistry
q: Universal indicator turns red in solution P, green in Q and violet in R. Which correctly identifies them?
options: P neutral, Q acidic, R basic
P strongly acidic, Q neutral, R strongly basic
P strongly basic, Q neutral, R strongly acidic
explanation: Universal indicator shows the whole pH range: red (pH ≈ 1–2, strong acid), orange/yellow (weak acid), green (pH 7, neutral), blue (weak base) and violet/purple (pH ≈ 13–14, strong base).
hints: Green is in the middle of the scale.

subject: Chemistry
q: A turmeric-stained cloth turns reddish-brown when washed with soap. What does this tell you about the soap solution?
explanation: Turmeric is a natural indicator: yellow in acidic and neutral solutions, reddish-brown in basic ones. Soap solutions are mildly basic.
hints: Turmeric changes colour with which type of solution?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which salt, made by passing chlorine gas over dry slaked lime, is used to disinfect drinking water?
explanation: Cl₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O. Bleaching powder releases chlorine, which kills microbes in water and bleaches cotton and linen.
hints: Which compound releases chlorine?

subject: Chemistry
q: What is washing soda, and what is one of its uses?
options: Sodium carbonate decahydrate (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O); removing permanent hardness of water
explanation: Washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O. Its carbonate ions precipitate the calcium and magnesium ions that make water hard, and it is used in cleaning and in making glass. Baking soda is NaHCO₃.
misconception: Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) and baking soda (NaHCO₃) are different compounds.
hints: It contains ten molecules of water of crystallisation.

subject: Chemistry
q: Acid rain has lowered the pH of a mountain lake to about 5, and fish populations are falling. Which action would directly address the chemical cause in the lake?
options: Adding vinegar to balance the pH
Adding more water from the same rainfall
Adding powdered limestone (calcium carbonate) to neutralise the acid
Adding table salt to the lake
explanation: Calcium carbonate is a base: CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂, raising pH towards neutral. Liming is used in parts of Scandinavia. It treats the symptom; the lasting solution is cutting SO₂ and NOₓ emissions that cause acid rain.
hints: What substance neutralises acid without harming the water?
Which option is a base?

subject: Chemistry
q: A metal can be beaten into thin sheets and drawn into thin wires. These properties are called:
explanation: Malleable means it can be hammered into sheets; ductile means it can be drawn into wires. Gold is the most malleable and ductile metal — one gram can be drawn into a wire about 2 km long.
hints: Sheets → malleable; wires → ?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why are cooking pans made of metal but fitted with plastic or wooden handles?
options: Plastic handles make the pan heavier.
Metals conduct heat well to cook food; plastic and wood are poor conductors, so the handle stays cool.
Wood conducts heat better than metal.
explanation: Metals have free electrons that carry heat quickly, ideal for transferring heat to food. Plastic and wood are insulators, protecting the cook’s hand.
hints: Which materials conduct heat well?

subject: Chemistry
q: How is the bond formed between sodium and chlorine in sodium chloride?
options: They are held by a metallic bond
Chlorine gives an electron to sodium
Sodium and chlorine share a pair of electrons
Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by electrostatic attraction
explanation: Na (2, 8, 1) loses its outer electron and Cl (2, 8, 7) gains it, giving both a stable octet. The oppositely charged ions attract strongly in all directions, forming an ionic lattice with a high melting point (801 °C).
misconception: Sharing electrons is covalent bonding, typical of non-metal with non-metal.
hints: Which atom has one electron to lose, and which needs one more?

subject: Chemistry
q: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride and its solution in water do. Why?
options: Water conducts electricity by itself strongly.
In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice; when molten or dissolved, the ions are free to move and carry charge.
explanation: Electric current needs mobile charge carriers. In solid NaCl the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are locked in place. Melting or dissolving frees the ions to move towards the electrodes, so the liquid or solution conducts (and is decomposed — electrolysis).
misconception: Ionic compounds conduct by moving IONS, not free electrons as metals do.
hints: What must be free to move for a substance to conduct?

subject: Chemistry
q: Iron nails are kept for a week in three test tubes: (A) dry air with calcium chloride to absorb moisture; (B) boiled water covered with a layer of oil; (C) ordinary tap water open to air. Only the nail in C rusts. What can be concluded?
options: Rusting needs both oxygen (air) and water.
explanation: Tube A has air but no water; tube B has water but no dissolved air (boiling removes it and oil stops it re-dissolving). Neither nail rusts. Only C has both, so both oxygen and water are necessary.
hints: What is missing from each tube that does not rust?

subject: Chemistry
q: Galvanised iron (coated with zinc) does not rust even where the zinc coating is scratched and the iron is exposed. Why?
options: The scratch fills with zinc again.
Zinc makes the iron less reactive permanently.
Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes in preference and protects the iron (sacrificial protection).
explanation: Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series. When both are exposed to water and air, zinc gives up electrons more readily and is oxidised instead of the iron. A plain paint coating, by contrast, stops protecting as soon as it is scratched.
misconception: Zinc protects not only as a barrier but also chemically, by being sacrificed.
hints: Which metal is more reactive: zinc or iron?
Which metal will lose electrons first?

subject: Chemistry
q: Brass, used in musical instruments and door fittings, is an alloy of:
explanation: Brass = copper + zinc. Bronze = copper + tin. Steel = iron + carbon (and often other metals). Solder = lead + tin (lead-free solders now use tin with silver or copper). Alloys are often harder and more corrosion-resistant than the pure metals.
misconception: Bronze, not brass, is copper and tin.
hints: Bronze is copper and tin — brass is different.

subject: Chemistry
q: Why is gold often found as the pure metal in nature, while sodium never is?
options: Gold is very unreactive, while sodium reacts readily with oxygen and water.
explanation: Metals at the bottom of the reactivity series (gold, platinum) resist reacting with air and water, so they survive uncombined for millions of years. Highly reactive metals like sodium exist only in compounds such as rock salt.
hints: Where are gold and sodium in the reactivity series?

subject: Chemistry
q: Iron is extracted by heating its oxide with carbon, but aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of molten alumina. Why can carbon not be used for aluminium?
options: Aluminium is found as the pure metal.
Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot take oxygen away from aluminium oxide.
explanation: A reducing agent can remove oxygen only from a metal less reactive than itself. Carbon is more reactive than iron but less reactive than aluminium. So aluminium needs the much more energy-intensive route of electrolysis — why recycling aluminium saves so much energy.
hints: Can a less reactive element remove oxygen from a more reactive one?

subject: Chemistry
q: In the thermite reaction, Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃, so much heat is released that the iron produced is molten. What is it used for?
options: Welding railway tracks and broken machine parts
explanation: Aluminium is more reactive than iron, so it displaces iron from its oxide in a highly exothermic reaction. The molten iron flows into the gap between rails and solidifies, joining them.
hints: What can molten iron be used to join?

subject: Chemistry
q: Haematite ore is mainly iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃. What percentage of the mass of pure Fe₂O₃ is iron? (Fe = 56, O = 16)
explanation: Molar mass = 2 × 56 + 3 × 16 = 112 + 48 = 160 g/mol. Iron = 112/160 × 100 = 70%. So at most 700 kg of iron can be obtained from each tonne of pure Fe₂O₃.
misconception: 35% counts only one iron atom; 77.8% is the value for FeO.
hints: How many iron atoms are in one formula unit of Fe₂O₃?
% = mass of Fe ÷ molar mass × 100.

subject: Chemistry
q: Copper roofs and statues (like the Statue of Liberty) slowly turn green. What forms on the surface?
options: Basic copper carbonate, from reaction with oxygen, water and carbon dioxide in the air
Copper oxide only, which is green
explanation: In moist air containing CO₂, copper slowly forms a green layer (patina) of basic copper carbonate, CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂. It protects the metal underneath. Copper oxide formed by heating is black.
hints: Which three substances in air are involved?

subject: Chemistry
q: Carbon has four valence electrons. How does it usually form bonds?
explanation: Losing or gaining four electrons would need too much energy (forming C⁴⁺ or C⁴⁻). Instead, carbon shares its four electrons, forming four covalent bonds — it is tetravalent, as in methane (CH₄).
hints: Is it easy to gain or lose four electrons?

subject: Chemistry
q: Millions of carbon compounds are known — far more than for any other element. Which property mainly explains this?
options: Catenation: carbon atoms form strong bonds with each other, giving long chains, branches and rings.
Carbon is the most abundant element.
explanation: Carbon–carbon bonds are strong and stable, so carbon can link into chains and rings of almost any length. Combined with its valency of 4 (allowing branches and bonds to H, O, N and others), this gives enormous variety.
hints: What can carbon atoms do with each other?

subject: Chemistry
q: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) and ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) both contain two carbon atoms. Which functional groups do they contain?
explanation: The functional group decides a compound’s chemistry. –OH makes ethanol an alcohol (neutral, burns cleanly). –COOH makes ethanoic acid a weak acid (vinegar is 5–8% ethanoic acid).
hints: Which compound is an acid?

subject: Chemistry
q: How many different structural isomers have the formula C₄H₁₀?
explanation: Four carbons can be arranged as a straight chain (butane) or as a three-carbon chain with a branch on the middle carbon (2-methylpropane, isobutane). Any other drawing is one of these two. Isomers have the same formula but different structures and properties.
misconception: Bending a chain on paper does not create a new isomer.
hints: Try a straight chain and a branched chain.

subject: Chemistry
q: Bromine water (orange) is shaken separately with two hydrocarbons. With hydrocarbon X it stays orange; with Y it quickly becomes colourless. What can be concluded?
options: X is unsaturated; Y is saturated.
Y is unsaturated (contains a C=C double bond); X is saturated.
explanation: Bromine adds across carbon–carbon double bonds (addition reaction), decolourising bromine water. Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) have only single bonds and do not react in this way under normal conditions.
hints: Which kind of bond can bromine add across?

subject: Chemistry
q: What is the molar mass of ethanol, C₂H₅OH? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
explanation: C₂H₅OH contains 2 C, 6 H (5 + 1) and 1 O: 2 × 12 + 6 × 1 + 16 = 46 g/mol.
misconception: 45 g/mol forgets the hydrogen in the –OH group.
hints: Count all the hydrogen atoms, including the one in –OH.

subject: Chemistry
q: A gas stove burning with a yellow, sooty flame is producing more carbon monoxide than usual. What is the most likely cause?
options: Too much oxygen is reaching the fuel.
Not enough oxygen is reaching the fuel, so combustion is incomplete.
explanation: With plenty of oxygen, hydrocarbons burn completely to CO₂ and H₂O with a clean blue flame. With limited oxygen, combustion is incomplete, producing soot (glowing carbon particles make the flame yellow) and poisonous carbon monoxide. Blocked air holes should be cleaned.
hints: What does incomplete combustion produce?

subject: Chemistry
q: Carbon monoxide from a faulty heater in a closed room can kill without any warning smell. Why is it so dangerous to the body?
options: It makes the blood too thick to flow.
It is a strong acid that burns the lungs.
It blocks sound reaching the ears.
It binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen, so the blood carries much less oxygen.
explanation: Haemoglobin binds CO about 200–250 times more strongly than O₂, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. Even a small concentration of CO greatly reduces the oxygen the blood can carry, starving the brain and heart. CO is colourless and odourless — hence CO detectors and good ventilation.
hints: Which molecule in red blood cells normally carries oxygen?
What happens if another gas occupies its binding sites?

subject: Chemistry
q: Vegetable oils are converted into solid vanaspati ghee by heating with hydrogen in the presence of nickel. What is this process?
options: Hydrogenation — an addition reaction that saturates C=C double bonds
explanation: Unsaturated oils have C=C double bonds. With a nickel catalyst, hydrogen adds across them, making the fats more saturated and solid at room temperature. Diets high in saturated and trans fats are linked to heart disease.
hints: What is added to the oil?

subject: Chemistry
q: Ethanol and ethanoic acid are warmed with a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid. A sweet, fruity smell is produced. What has formed?
explanation: Alcohol + carboxylic acid → ester + water (esterification), with sulphuric acid as a catalyst. Esters give many fruits and perfumes their smells.
hints: Many fruit smells come from this class of compound.

subject: Chemistry
q: How does soap remove an oily stain from cloth?
options: Soap dissolves the cloth around the stain.
Soap reacts with oil to form water.
Soap makes oil denser than water so it sinks.
Soap molecules point their hydrocarbon tails into the oil and their ionic heads into the water, forming micelles that are rinsed away.
explanation: A soap molecule has a long hydrophobic (oil-loving) tail and an ionic hydrophilic (water-loving) head. In water they cluster around oil droplets with tails inside the oil and heads outside, forming micelles. The micelles stay suspended in water and wash away.
hints: A soap molecule has two very different ends.

subject: Chemistry
q: Diamond, graphite and buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) are all pure carbon with very different properties. They are called:
explanation: Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element. Isotopes are atoms with different numbers of neutrons; isomers are different compounds with the same formula; alloys are mixtures of metals.
misconception: Isotopes differ in neutrons; allotropes differ in how atoms are bonded together.
hints: Different forms of the same element in the same state.

subject: Chemistry
q: Why are pickles preserved with plenty of salt or oil?
options: Salt draws water out of microbes by osmosis, and oil keeps air out, so microbes cannot grow.
Salt reacts with the vegetables to make plastic.
explanation: A high salt concentration makes microbial cells lose water by osmosis, killing or inactivating them. A layer of oil cuts off the oxygen most spoilage microbes need and slows oxidation.
hints: What happens to a cell in a very salty solution?

subject: Chemistry
q: Milk of magnesia relieves acidity in the stomach. What kind of substance is it, and what does it do?
options: A salt that adds more acid
A mild base (magnesium hydroxide) that neutralises excess hydrochloric acid
A sugar that coats the stomach
explanation: The stomach produces hydrochloric acid for digestion. Excess acid causes indigestion. Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O neutralises some of it. A strong base would damage the stomach lining, so a mild one is used.
hints: What neutralises an acid?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why should water NOT be thrown onto a burning pan of cooking oil?
options: Water reacts with oil to make an explosive gas.
Water is too cold to work.
Water sinks under the hot oil, turns instantly to steam and throws burning oil out, spreading the fire.
Water makes oil burn hotter by adding oxygen.
explanation: Oil is less dense than water and hotter than 100 °C. Water sinks below it, boils explosively and sprays burning oil droplets into the air. Instead, turn off the heat and cover the pan with a lid or damp cloth to cut off oxygen.
hints: Which is denser, water or oil — and what happens to water above 100 °C?

subject: Chemistry
q: Blowing on a candle flame puts it out, but blowing on glowing charcoal embers makes them burn brighter. Which explanation fits both observations?
options: Candles cannot burn in moving air.
Blowing on the candle carries away the hot wax vapour and heat it needs; blowing on embers supplies extra oxygen to fuel that is already hot.
explanation: Fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen (the fire triangle). A candle burns wax VAPOUR; blowing removes the vapour and cools the wick below ignition temperature, so the flame dies. Embers are solid, very hot fuel that is short of oxygen; extra air speeds up their combustion.
misconception: Breath still contains about 16% oxygen — enough to feed embers.
hints: What three things does a fire need?
Which of these does blowing remove in each case, and which does it add?

subject: Chemistry
q: Water that does not lather easily with soap is called hard water. What does it contain?
explanation: Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions (from hydrogencarbonates, sulphates and chlorides) picked up from rocks. These ions react with soap to form insoluble scum instead of lather.
hints: Which metal ions come from limestone and similar rocks?

subject: Chemistry
q: Boiling removes the hardness of some water samples but not others. What kind of hardness does boiling remove?
options: Permanent hardness, caused by calcium sulphate
Temporary hardness, caused by calcium and magnesium hydrogencarbonates
explanation: On boiling, Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂O + CO₂: the dissolved calcium precipitates as limescale (the white crust in kettles). Chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium (permanent hardness) do not decompose and need washing soda or ion exchange.
hints: Which compounds decompose on heating to form an insoluble carbonate?

subject: Chemistry
q: NPK fertilisers supply nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Which nutrient is needed mainly for healthy green leaves and growth?
explanation: Nitrogen is part of every amino acid (proteins) and of chlorophyll, so it drives leafy growth; shortage causes yellowing leaves. Phosphorus is important for roots and energy transfer (ATP); potassium for flowering, fruiting and disease resistance.
hints: Which element is part of chlorophyll and proteins?

subject: Chemistry
q: Urea, CO(NH₂)₂, is India’s most widely used nitrogen fertiliser. What percentage of its mass is nitrogen? (C = 12, O = 16, N = 14, H = 1)
explanation: Molar mass = 12 + 16 + 2 × (14 + 2) = 60 g/mol. It contains two N atoms: 28 g. % N = 28/60 × 100 ≈ 46.7% — higher than ammonium nitrate (35%), which is one reason urea is popular.
misconception: 23.3% counts only one nitrogen atom.
hints: How many N atoms are in CO(NH₂)₂?
Work out the molar mass carefully.

subject: Chemistry
q: Why is common salt sold in India “iodised”?
options: The thyroid gland needs iodine to make the hormone thyroxine; deficiency causes goitre.
Iodine adds sodium to the diet.
explanation: Iodine is an essential part of thyroxine, which controls metabolism. Lack of iodine causes the thyroid to enlarge (goitre) and, in children, can impair development. Adding a small amount of potassium iodate or iodide to salt is a cheap way to prevent it.
hints: Which gland swells in goitre?

subject: Chemistry
q: Ordinary window glass is made mainly by melting together:
explanation: Soda-lime glass is made by melting silica sand with sodium carbonate (to lower the melting point) and limestone (to make it durable), at around 1500 °C, then cooling it without letting it crystallise.
hints: The main raw material is found on beaches.

subject: Chemistry
q: A bottle of soda water fizzes much more when opened warm than when opened cold from the fridge. Why?
options: Gases are less soluble in warmer water, so more dissolved CO₂ comes out when the pressure is released.
Sugar stops CO₂ escaping when cold.
Cold water reacts with CO₂ to form a solid.
explanation: The drink is bottled with CO₂ under pressure. Opening the bottle lowers the pressure, so dissolved gas comes out of solution. Gas solubility falls as temperature rises, so a warm drink holds less CO₂ in solution and releases it much faster — and goes flat sooner.
hints: How does temperature affect how much gas water can dissolve?
What happens to pressure when the cap is removed?

subject: Chemistry
q: LPG has almost no smell of its own, yet a gas leak smells strongly. Why?
options: LPG reacts with air to form a smell.
The smell comes from the steel cylinder.
A strong-smelling sulphur compound (a mercaptan) is added so leaks can be detected.
explanation: LPG (mainly propane and butane) is odourless. A small amount of ethyl mercaptan, which has a strong smell, is added so that a dangerous leak can be noticed before it builds up to an explosive concentration.
hints: The smell is added deliberately — why?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why does baking powder (baking soda mixed with a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid) give better-tasting cakes than baking soda alone?
options: The acid reacts with the baking soda to release CO₂ and prevents the bitter-tasting sodium carbonate from forming.
The acid makes the cake sour.
Baking soda alone does not release any gas.
explanation: Heated alone, 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂: the sodium carbonate left behind tastes bitter and soapy. With an acid present, NaHCO₃ is neutralised, releasing CO₂ without leaving sodium carbonate, so the cake rises and tastes better.
misconception: Baking soda alone does release CO₂ on heating — the problem is the leftover product.
hints: What does baking soda leave behind when it decomposes on its own?

subject: Chemistry
q: Many water purifiers contain activated charcoal. How does it remove bad tastes, odours and some chemicals?
options: It kills bacteria by heating the water.
It adds chlorine to the water.
Its enormous internal surface area adsorbs (holds on its surface) many impurity molecules.
explanation: Activated charcoal is riddled with tiny pores — one gram can have a surface area of several hundred square metres. Organic molecules and some gases stick to this surface (adsorption) and are removed from the water. It does not reliably remove all microbes or dissolved salts.
misconception: Adsorption (onto a surface) is different from absorption (into the bulk).
hints: Why is the charcoal “activated” — what does that do to its surface?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why is chlorine added to municipal drinking water supplies?
options: To make the water taste sweet
explanation: Chlorine (or chlorine compounds such as bleaching powder) is a powerful disinfectant that kills bacteria and many viruses, preventing water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
hints: Which diseases spread through dirty water?

subject: Chemistry
q: A spoonful of sugar is dissolved completely in a glass of water filled to a marked level. The water level barely rises. What does this suggest?
options: Sugar is destroyed when it dissolves.
There are spaces between water particles into which sugar particles fit.
explanation: Sugar particles spread out and occupy spaces between water particles, so the total volume increases far less than the volumes of sugar and water added separately. This is evidence that matter is made of particles with spaces between them. The mass still increases by the mass of sugar.
misconception: Dissolved sugar is still there — taste the water.
hints: Where do the sugar particles go?

subject: Chemistry
q: Under a microscope, tiny pollen grains suspended in water are seen jiggling randomly, even though the water is still. What causes this “Brownian motion”?
options: The pollen grains are alive and swimming
Uneven bombardment of the grains by fast-moving, invisible water molecules
explanation: Water molecules move randomly and constantly collide with the grains. At any instant more hit one side than the other, pushing the grain in a random direction. Brownian motion (explained by Einstein in 1905) was key evidence that molecules really exist. Non-living dust particles show it too.
misconception: The motion occurs with non-living particles as well, so it is not swimming.
hints: What invisible particles surround the grains?

subject: Chemistry
q: A gas in a syringe occupies 2 L at a pressure of 1 atmosphere. It is slowly compressed to 0.5 L at constant temperature. What is its new pressure?
explanation: Boyle’s law: at constant temperature, pressure × volume is constant: 1 × 2 = P × 0.5, so P = 4 atm. Squeezing the same particles into a quarter of the space makes them hit the walls four times as often.
misconception: 0.25 atm assumes pressure falls as volume falls; they are inversely related.
hints: At constant temperature, P × V stays the same.
Volume becomes a quarter — what happens to the collisions on the walls?

subject: Chemistry
q: A balloon left in hot sunlight swells and may burst. Why?
options: Heating makes gas particles move faster; at nearly constant pressure the gas expands.
Sunlight adds more gas to the balloon.
explanation: Heating raises the kinetic energy of the gas particles, so they hit the balloon wall harder and more often, and the balloon expands until the pressure inside again matches the stretched rubber. Charles’s law: at constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature.
hints: What happens to particle speed when a gas is heated?

subject: Chemistry
q: In which state of matter does diffusion happen fastest?
options: It is equally fast in all states
explanation: Gas particles move fastest and have the most space between them, so they mix quickly — a perfume spreads across a room in minutes. Diffusion in liquids is slower, and in solids extremely slow.
hints: Where are particles most free to move?

subject: Chemistry
q: Water stored in an unglazed earthen pot (matka) stays cooler than water in a metal jug. Why?
options: Water seeps through the pores and evaporates from the outer surface, taking latent heat from the pot and the water inside.
Metal jugs absorb cold from the air.
explanation: Evaporation needs latent heat. As water evaporates from the pot’s moist outer surface, it draws this heat from the pot and the water inside, lowering their temperature. The effect is strongest in dry weather, when evaporation is fastest.
hints: Which process absorbs heat from its surroundings?

subject: Chemistry
q: You feel much hotter and stickier on a humid day at 35 °C than on a dry day at the same temperature. Why?
options: Humid air is hotter than the thermometer shows.
Humid air already holds a lot of water vapour, so sweat evaporates slowly and cools you less.
Sweat production stops on humid days.
explanation: Sweating cools us only when the sweat evaporates, because evaporation takes latent heat from the skin. The rate of evaporation falls as the air approaches saturation with water vapour. On a humid day sweat stays on the skin, so cooling is poor.
hints: How does sweat cool the body?
What slows down evaporation?

subject: Chemistry
q: Water droplets appear on the outside of a glass filled with ice-cold water. Where do they come from?
options: Water seeps out through the glass.
The ice melts through the glass.
Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold surface.
The glass produces water when cold.
explanation: Air contains water vapour. When it touches the cold glass, it cools below its dew point and condenses into liquid droplets. Glass is impermeable, so the water cannot come from inside.
hints: Is glass permeable to water?

subject: Chemistry
q: Matter in the Sun and in a glowing neon sign exists largely as plasma. What is plasma?
options: A hot, ionised gas containing free electrons and positive ions
explanation: When a gas is heated to very high temperature or energised by electricity, electrons are stripped from atoms, giving a mixture of ions and free electrons. Plasma conducts electricity and glows; it is often called the fourth state of matter.
hints: What happens to atoms when they are given a huge amount of energy?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why does hot tea poured into a wide saucer cool faster than tea in a narrow cup?
options: Tea in a saucer has more heat.
Saucers are made of colder material.
The larger surface area allows faster evaporation, which removes heat.
explanation: Evaporation happens at the surface. Spreading the tea in a saucer exposes much more surface to the air, so evaporation — and the cooling it causes — is faster. Greater contact with the air also speeds heat loss by convection.
hints: Where does evaporation take place?

subject: Chemistry
q: How many moles are present in 4 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH? (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
misconception: 10 mol divides the wrong way.
hints: n = mass ÷ molar mass.

subject: Chemistry
q: How many atoms in total are present in 0.1 mol of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄? (Avogadro constant = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
explanation: 0.1 mol contains 0.1 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 6.022 × 10²² molecules. Each molecule has 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 atoms, so total atoms = 7 × 6.022 × 10²² ≈ 4.22 × 10²³.
misconception: 6.02 × 10²² is the number of MOLECULES, not atoms.
hints: First find the number of molecules.
How many atoms are in one H₂SO₄ molecule?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which postulate of Dalton’s atomic theory is now known to be incorrect?
options: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions.
Atoms are indivisible and cannot be broken into smaller particles.
Atoms of different elements have different masses.
Atoms combine in small whole-number ratios.
explanation: Atoms are made of protons, neutrons and electrons, and can be split in nuclear reactions. Dalton’s other ideas still hold in chemistry. (His claim that all atoms of an element are identical in mass also needed correction after isotopes were discovered.)
hints: What are atoms made of?

subject: Chemistry
q: Calcium has valency 2 and the phosphate ion (PO₄) has valency 3. What is the formula of calcium phosphate, the main mineral in bones?
explanation: Criss-cross the valencies: 3 Ca²⁺ give +6 and 2 PO₄³⁻ give −6. Ca₃(PO₄)₂ is neutral.
misconception: Ca₂(PO₄)₃ swaps the numbers; check that the total charge is zero.
hints: Total positive charge must equal total negative charge.

subject: Chemistry
q: What mass of oxygen is needed to burn 12 g of carbon completely to carbon dioxide? (C + O₂ → CO₂; C = 12, O = 16)
explanation: 12 g of carbon is 1 mol. The equation is 1 : 1, so 1 mol O₂ = 32 g is needed, forming 44 g of CO₂ (mass is conserved: 12 + 32 = 44).
misconception: 44 g is the mass of CO₂ produced, not of oxygen needed.
hints: Convert 12 g of carbon to moles.
How many moles of O₂ react with each mole of C?

subject: Chemistry
q: The symbols Na, K and Fe come from the Latin names of the elements. Which set gives the correct elements?
options: Na = sodium, K = potassium, Fe = iron
Na = nitrogen, K = krypton, Fe = fluorine
Na = nickel, K = potassium, Fe = fermium
Na = neon, K = calcium, Fe = phosphorus
explanation: Na from natrium (sodium), K from kalium (potassium), Fe from ferrum (iron). Other examples: Cu (cuprum, copper), Ag (argentum, silver), Au (aurum, gold), Pb (plumbum, lead).
hints: “Ferrous” metals contain iron.

subject: Chemistry
q: The ammonium ion is NH₄⁺ (valency 1) and the sulphate ion is SO₄²⁻. What is the formula of ammonium sulphate, a common fertiliser?
explanation: Two NH₄⁺ ions (+2 total) balance one SO₄²⁻ (−2). Brackets show that the whole ammonium group is taken twice: (NH₄)₂SO₄.
hints: How many +1 ions are needed to balance one −2 ion?

subject: Chemistry
q: In carbon monoxide, 12 g of carbon is combined with 16 g of oxygen. In carbon dioxide, 12 g of carbon is combined with 32 g of oxygen. What does the ratio of these oxygen masses illustrate?
options: The law of multiple proportions: the masses of oxygen combining with a fixed mass of carbon are in a simple whole-number ratio (1 : 2).
The law of conservation of mass
That carbon has two different atomic masses
explanation: For a fixed 12 g of carbon, oxygen masses are 16 g and 32 g, a 1 : 2 ratio. This simple whole-number relationship (Dalton’s law of multiple proportions) is explained by atoms combining as whole units: CO has one O per C, CO₂ has two.
hints: Compare the two oxygen masses for the same 12 g of carbon.
Why should the ratio be a simple whole number if atoms exist?

subject: Chemistry
q: What is the atomicity (number of atoms per molecule) of ozone and of phosphorus (in its common white form)?
explanation: Ozone is O₃ (triatomic); white phosphorus exists as P₄ molecules (tetra-atomic); sulphur as S₈. Noble gases are monatomic; oxygen and nitrogen are diatomic (O₂, N₂).
hints: Ozone is a form of oxygen with one more atom than O₂.

subject: Chemistry
q: What is the mass in grams of a single carbon-12 atom? (Avogadro constant = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
explanation: One mole of carbon-12 (6.022 × 10²³ atoms) has a mass of 12 g, so one atom has a mass of 12 / 6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 1.99 × 10⁻²³ g. Atoms are unimaginably light — which is exactly why chemists count them in moles.
hints: Divide the molar mass by the number of atoms in a mole.

subject: Chemistry
q: Who discovered the electron through experiments with cathode rays?
explanation: In 1897 J. J. Thomson showed that cathode rays are streams of tiny negatively charged particles, much lighter than atoms — electrons. Rutherford discovered the nucleus (1911), Chadwick the neutron (1932), and Bohr proposed energy levels (1913).
hints: He also proposed the “plum-pudding” model.

subject: Chemistry
q: E. Goldstein observed “canal rays” travelling in the opposite direction to cathode rays in a discharge tube. What did this lead to?
options: The discovery of positively charged particles, later identified as protons
explanation: Canal rays (1886) were positively charged and moved towards the cathode, showing that atoms also contain positive charge. The lightest such particle, from hydrogen, was later named the proton by Rutherford.
hints: Cathode rays are negative; canal rays move the opposite way.

subject: Chemistry
q: Using the 2n² rule, what is the maximum number of electrons the L shell (n = 2) can hold?
explanation: 2n² = 2 × 2² = 8. The K shell (n = 1) holds 2, the L shell 8, the M shell (n = 3) up to 18 — although an outermost shell never holds more than 8.
hints: Substitute n = 2 into 2n².

subject: Chemistry
q: An element has three electron shells and three valence electrons. What is its atomic number?
explanation: Three shells with the first two full: 2, 8, then 3 in the outer shell — 13 electrons, so Z = 13 (aluminium).
hints: Fill K and L completely, then add the valence electrons.

subject: Chemistry
q: Magnesium has atomic number 12. What is its valency?
explanation: Mg is 2, 8, 2. It achieves a stable octet most easily by losing its two outer electrons, forming Mg²⁺, so its valency is 2.
misconception: 6 counts the electrons it would need to GAIN — far harder than losing 2.
hints: Write the configuration of Z = 12.

subject: Chemistry
q: An ion X²⁻ contains 18 electrons. What is the atomic number of element X?
explanation: The 2− charge means X has gained 2 electrons. The neutral atom therefore has 18 − 2 = 16 electrons and 16 protons: Z = 16 (sulphur, forming S²⁻).
misconception: 20 adds the charge instead of subtracting it.
hints: A negative ion has GAINED electrons.
How many electrons did the neutral atom have?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which pairing of a radioactive isotope with its use is correct?
explanation: Cobalt-60 emits gamma rays used to destroy cancer cells. Other examples: iodine-131 (thyroid disorders), uranium-235 (fuel in nuclear reactors), carbon-14 (dating). Carbon-12, iodine-127 and hydrogen-1 are stable, non-radioactive isotopes.
hints: Which isotope listed is radioactive?

subject: Chemistry
q: When sodium salts are heated in a flame they give a bright yellow colour; copper salts give blue-green. How does Bohr’s model explain these specific colours?
options: Different metals reflect different colours of the flame.
Electrons absorb energy, jump to higher energy levels, and emit light of particular energies (colours) when they fall back.
Nuclei split and give out coloured light.
The flame burns the metal into a coloured gas.
explanation: In Bohr’s model, electrons occupy fixed energy levels. Heat excites them to higher levels; when they return, they emit light whose energy equals the gap between levels. Each element has different gaps, so it emits its own characteristic colours — the basis of flame tests and fireworks.
hints: In Bohr’s model, can electrons have any energy?
What is given out when an electron drops to a lower level?

subject: Chemistry
q: If an atom were enlarged to the size of a cricket stadium, the nucleus would be roughly the size of:
explanation: The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller in diameter than the atom (about 10⁻¹⁵ m vs 10⁻¹⁰ m), yet holds over 99.9% of its mass. A stadium-sized atom (≈ 100–200 m across) would have a nucleus of a millimetre or two — about the size of a pea or smaller.
hints: The nucleus is about 1/100,000 of the atom’s diameter.

subject: Chemistry
q: Which pair of particles has the same number of electrons (is isoelectronic)?
explanation: Na (11 electrons) loses one to become Na⁺ with 10 electrons, the same as neon (10). Cl has 17 electrons and Ar 18; Mg has 12 and Na⁺ 10.
hints: Count electrons in each, remembering what a + charge means.

subject: Chemistry
q: Which property is typical of a true solution, such as sugar in water?
options: It can be separated by filtration
Particles are too small to see, do not settle and pass through filter paper
It scatters a beam of light strongly
explanation: In a true solution, solute particles are molecules or ions smaller than about 1 nm. They do not settle, pass through filter paper and do not scatter light noticeably. Suspensions settle and can be filtered; colloids scatter light.
hints: How small are the particles in a true solution?

subject: Chemistry
q: Chalk powder is stirred into water. After some time the chalk settles at the bottom, and it can be removed by filtering. What type of mixture is chalky water?
explanation: Suspensions contain particles large enough (usually over 1000 nm) to settle under gravity and be trapped by filter paper. They are heterogeneous and usually opaque.
hints: Particles that settle on standing belong to which type of mixture?

subject: Chemistry
q: At 20 °C, 36 g of salt dissolves in 100 g of water to make a saturated solution. What is the maximum mass of salt that can dissolve in 250 g of water at the same temperature?
explanation: Solubility scales with the mass of water: 36 g per 100 g → 36 × 2.5 = 90 g in 250 g of water.
misconception: 14.4 g divides by 2.5 instead of multiplying.
hints: 250 g of water is how many times 100 g?

subject: Chemistry
q: Acetone (boiling point 56 °C) and water (100 °C) mix completely. How can they be separated?
options: Distillation, collecting acetone first as it boils off at a lower temperature
explanation: The liquids are miscible, so a separating funnel will not work, and both pass through filter paper. Heating the mixture boils off acetone first; its vapour is condensed and collected, leaving water behind. Liquids with closer boiling points need fractional distillation.
misconception: A separating funnel only separates liquids that do NOT mix.
hints: Do the two liquids mix?
What property differs between them?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which apparatus is best for separating a mixture of kerosene and water?
explanation: Kerosene and water are immiscible and form two layers; kerosene, being less dense, floats on top. Opening the tap of a separating funnel drains off the lower water layer.
hints: Do kerosene and water mix?

subject: Chemistry
q: Impure copper sulphate is purified by crystallisation rather than by simply evaporating its solution to dryness. Why is crystallisation better?
options: Soluble impurities stay dissolved in the remaining liquid, and the crystals keep their water of crystallisation instead of decomposing.
Evaporation makes copper sulphate change colour permanently into a new element.
explanation: Evaporating to dryness leaves every dissolved impurity in the solid and can overheat the salt, driving off its water of crystallisation (blue CuSO₄·5H₂O becomes white anhydrous CuSO₄). In crystallisation, the solution is concentrated and cooled; pure crystals form while impurities remain in the mother liquor, which is filtered off.
hints: Where do the soluble impurities end up in each method?
What happens to hydrated crystals when heated strongly?

subject: Chemistry
q: How are nitrogen, oxygen and argon obtained from air on an industrial scale?
options: By fractional distillation of liquefied air, using their different boiling points
explanation: Air is a mixture, so its components keep their own boiling points. It is cooled and compressed until it liquefies (below about −200 °C), then warmed gradually in a fractionating column: nitrogen (−196 °C) boils off first, then argon (−186 °C), then oxygen (−183 °C).
hints: Air is a mixture — which property can separate its parts?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which is correctly matched as a colloid of the given type?
options: Shaving foam — solid dispersed in gas
explanation: Fog and clouds are tiny water droplets (liquid) dispersed in air (gas). Smoke is solid particles in gas; shaving foam is gas dispersed in liquid; milk is liquid in liquid (an emulsion).
hints: Fog is made of tiny droplets floating in air.

subject: Chemistry
q: Brass looks perfectly uniform, yet chemists classify it as a mixture, not a compound. Which evidence supports this?
options: Its composition can vary (different brasses have different copper : zinc ratios) and it keeps properties of its metals.
It is made by a chemical reaction that releases gas.
It has a fixed chemical formula.
Its components cannot be separated by any method.
explanation: A compound has a fixed composition and new properties. Brass can contain anywhere from about 55% to 95% copper, and its properties change gradually with composition. It is a homogeneous mixture (a solid solution) of copper and zinc.
misconception: Looking uniform (homogeneous) does not make something a compound — salt water looks uniform too.
hints: Does brass have a fixed composition?
Is looking uniform enough to make something a compound?

subject: Chemistry
q: Along India’s coasts, salt is obtained from sea water in shallow salt pans. Which separation method is used?
explanation: Sea water (about 3.5% dissolved salts) is let into shallow pans. The Sun and wind evaporate the water, leaving crystals of salt, which are scraped up and purified.
hints: How does the water leave the pans?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which element in Period 3 has the largest atomic radius?
explanation: Atomic radius decreases across a period as the nuclear charge increases while electrons fill the same shell. Sodium, at the start of Period 3, has the largest radius.
hints: How does atomic radius change across a period?

subject: Chemistry
q: A nitrogen atom (2, 5) needs three more electrons for an octet. How are the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule, N₂, bonded?
options: By a triple covalent bond (three shared pairs)
explanation: Each nitrogen shares three of its electrons with the other, giving three shared pairs — a triple bond — and each atom an octet. This very strong bond makes N₂ unreactive, which is why nitrogen fixation needs special bacteria or a lot of energy.
hints: How many electrons does each N atom need to share?

subject: Chemistry
q: Why are covalent compounds such as sugar and petrol generally poor conductors of electricity?
options: They are made of neutral molecules and contain no free ions or electrons to carry charge.
explanation: Covalent compounds consist of molecules held together by shared electrons, which are not free to move. With no mobile charged particles, they cannot carry a current, even when molten or dissolved (sugar solution does not conduct).
hints: What carries charge in a conductor?

subject: Chemistry
q: In the chlor-alkali process, electricity is passed through brine (concentrated sodium chloride solution). Which products form?
options: Sodium metal at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
Chlorine at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode, and sodium hydroxide solution
explanation: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂. Chloride ions are oxidised to chlorine at the anode; water is reduced to hydrogen at the cathode, leaving sodium hydroxide in solution. All three products are industrially important (bleach, soap, PVC, fuel).
misconception: Sodium metal is not formed from a water solution because water is reduced in preference.
hints: The process is named after two of its products.

subject: Chemistry
q: Which noble gas is used to fill party balloons and airships because it is light and does not burn?
explanation: Helium is the second-lightest gas and, as a noble gas, completely non-flammable. Hydrogen is lighter but highly flammable (the Hindenburg airship disaster, 1937). Neon is used in glowing signs; argon fills filament bulbs.
misconception: Hydrogen is lighter but it is not a noble gas, and it burns.
hints: It must be light AND non-flammable.

subject: Chemistry
q: The smell of hot, freshly cooked food reaches you from across a room much faster than the smell of the same food when cold. Why?
options: Particles diffuse faster at higher temperature because they have more kinetic energy.
Hot food pushes the air towards you.
explanation: Smell reaches us by diffusion of vapour particles through air. At higher temperature the particles move faster (more kinetic energy) and more of them evaporate, so the aroma spreads faster.
misconception: Diffusion happens at all temperatures — heat speeds it up rather than causing it.
hints: How does temperature affect the speed of particles?

subject: Chemistry
q: While ice is melting at 0 °C, heat is continuously supplied but the thermometer reading does not rise. Where does the heat go?
options: It increases the kinetic energy of the particles.
It is lost to the surroundings.
It overcomes the forces of attraction between particles (latent heat of fusion).
It is stored as chemical energy in new bonds.
explanation: During a change of state, the energy supplied is used to break the attractions holding particles in the solid lattice rather than to make particles move faster. Temperature measures average kinetic energy, so it stays constant until all the ice has melted.
misconception: Constant temperature does not mean no energy is being absorbed — the energy is “hidden” (latent) in the change of state.
hints: What does temperature actually measure?

subject: Chemistry
q: On which day would wet clothes on a line dry fastest?
explanation: Evaporation is faster at higher temperature, lower humidity (air can hold more vapour) and with wind (which carries vapour away from the surface). All three favour a warm, dry, windy day.
misconception: Temperature alone is not enough: humid, still air slows evaporation a lot.
hints: List three factors that increase the rate of evaporation.

subject: Chemistry
q: Convert −40 °C to the Kelvin scale.
explanation: T(K) = T(°C) + 273 = −40 + 273 = 233 K. The Kelvin scale has no negative values because 0 K is absolute zero.
misconception: 313 K subtracts instead of adds the −40.

subject: Chemistry
q: Ice at −10 °C is heated at a constant rate until it has all turned to steam above 100 °C, and its temperature is plotted against time. The graph has two flat (horizontal) sections. Which is true?
options: Both flat sections are equally long.
The flat section at 0 °C is much longer than the one at 100 °C.
The flat section at 100 °C is much longer than the one at 0 °C.
The flat sections show that heat is being lost.
explanation: Flat sections are changes of state. Their lengths are proportional to the latent heat needed. The latent heat of vaporisation of water (≈ 2260 kJ/kg) is about 7 times its latent heat of fusion (≈ 334 kJ/kg), because boiling must separate particles completely, while melting only loosens them. So at a constant heating rate, boiling takes about 7 times longer.
misconception: Equal flat sections would require equal latent heats — but turning liquid into gas needs far more energy than melting.
hints: What determines how long each flat section lasts at a constant heating rate?
Which needs more energy: loosening particles or separating them completely?

subject: Chemistry
q: A block of dry ice (solid CO₂) left on a table gets smaller and produces a white fog, but no liquid puddle ever forms. Which process explains this?
explanation: At normal atmospheric pressure, solid CO₂ turns directly into gas (sublimation) at about −78 °C, without passing through a liquid state. The white fog is water vapour from the air condensing in the cold gas.
misconception: The fog is not CO₂ “steam” — CO₂ gas is invisible; the fog is condensed water from the air.
hints: Which change goes directly from solid to gas?

subject: Chemistry
q: How much energy is needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice already at 0 °C? (latent heat of fusion of ice = 334 kJ/kg)
explanation: Q = mL = 0.5 × 334 = 167 kJ. No temperature change is involved because the ice is already at its melting point.
misconception: 668 kJ multiplies by 2 instead of 0.5.
hints: Q = m × L.

subject: Chemistry
q:
Consider:
I. Gases are highly compressible because their particles are far apart.
II. Liquids diffuse faster than gases.
III. Solids have a definite shape and a definite volume.
IV. Particles of a solid do not move at all.
Which are correct?
explanation: I is true (large spaces between gas particles). II is false: gas particles move faster with more space, so gases diffuse faster than liquids. III is true. IV is false: particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions — they are never completely still above absolute zero.
misconception: “Fixed positions” in a solid does not mean motionless; the particles vibrate.
hints: Do the particles of a solid have any kinetic energy?

subject: Chemistry
q: What is the molar mass of sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄? (H = 1, S = 32, O = 16)
misconception: 96 g/mol forgets the two hydrogen atoms.
hints: Add up the masses of every atom in the formula.

subject: Chemistry
q: How many water molecules are in 9 g of water? (Avogadro constant = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
explanation: Molar mass of H₂O = 18 g/mol, so 9 g = 0.5 mol. Molecules = 0.5 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³.
misconception: 5.42 × 10²⁴ multiplies the mass (9) by Avogadro’s number instead of the number of moles.
hints: Convert grams to moles first: n = m/M.

subject: Chemistry
q: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
misconception: 400 g divides by 0.25 instead of multiplying.
hints: m = n × M.

subject: Chemistry
q: Which of the following contains the greatest number of ATOMS?
explanation: Count moles of atoms: H₂: 4/2 = 2 mol molecules × 2 = 4 mol atoms. O₂: 32/32 = 1 mol × 2 = 2 mol atoms. H₂O: 18/18 = 1 mol × 3 = 3 mol atoms. CO₂: 44/44 = 1 mol × 3 = 3 mol atoms. Hydrogen wins with 4 mol of atoms (≈ 2.4 × 10²⁴ atoms).
misconception: The largest mass does not mean the most atoms; light atoms like hydrogen give many atoms per gram.
hints: Convert each mass to moles of molecules.
Multiply by the number of atoms in each molecule.

subject: Chemistry
q: In water, hydrogen and oxygen always combine in the mass ratio 1 : 8. What mass of oxygen is needed to react completely with 3 g of hydrogen?
explanation: Law of constant proportions: mass ratio H : O = 1 : 8, so 3 g of hydrogen needs 3 × 8 = 24 g of oxygen, forming 27 g of water.
misconception: 27 g is the mass of water formed, not of oxygen needed.
hints: Scale the ratio 1 : 8 up by 3.

subject: Chemistry
q: Ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃) is used as a fertiliser. What percentage of its mass is nitrogen? (N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)
explanation: Molar mass = 14 + 4 + 14 + 48 = 80 g/mol. It contains TWO nitrogen atoms (one in NH₄⁺ and one in NO₃⁻): 28 g. Percentage = 28/80 × 100 = 35%.
misconception: 17.5% counts only one nitrogen atom — always count every atom of the element in the formula.
hints: How many N atoms are in NH₄NO₃?
% = (mass of N in formula ÷ molar mass) × 100.

subject: Chemistry
q: Aluminium has a valency of 3 and the sulphate ion (SO₄) has a valency of 2. What is the formula of aluminium sulphate?
explanation: Criss-cross the valencies: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ combine as 2 × (+3) = +6 and 3 × (−2) = −6, giving Al₂(SO₄)₃, which is electrically neutral.
misconception: Al₃(SO₄)₂ swaps the subscripts; check that the total charge is zero.
hints: Total positive charge must equal total negative charge.

subject: Chemistry
q: A magnesium ribbon is burnt in air and all the white ash is collected. The ash weighs MORE than the original ribbon. Does this violate the law of conservation of mass?
options: No — the balance must be faulty.
Yes — mass is created during combustion.
No — the ash includes oxygen from the air that combined with the magnesium.
explanation: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. The mass of magnesium oxide = mass of magnesium + mass of oxygen taken from the air. Total mass of all reactants (including the oxygen) equals the total mass of products, so mass is conserved.
misconception: When a reaction takes in a gas from the air, the solid product can weigh more than the starting solid.
hints: What does magnesium combine with when it burns?

subject: Chemistry
q: A compound contains 40% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. What is its simplest (empirical) formula? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
explanation: In 100 g: C = 40/12 = 3.33 mol, H = 6.7/1 = 6.7 mol, O = 53.3/16 = 3.33 mol. Dividing by the smallest (3.33): C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O. (Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, has this empirical formula.)
misconception: Mass percentages cannot be used directly as ratios — they must be converted to moles first.
hints: Assume 100 g of compound and convert each mass to moles.
Divide every mole value by the smallest one.

subject: Chemistry
q: In Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What did this show?
options: Most of the atom is empty space.
explanation: If the atom were a uniform solid ball, the particles would be blocked or deflected. Most passed straight through, so most of the atom must be empty space. The rare large deflections showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
misconception: The few particles that bounced back are the evidence for the nucleus; the many that passed through are the evidence for empty space.
hints: If the atom were a solid ball, what would happen to the alpha particles?

subject: Chemistry
q: Sodium has atomic number 11. What is the electronic configuration of the sodium ion, Na⁺?
explanation: A sodium atom is 2, 8, 1. It loses its single outer electron to form Na⁺, leaving 10 electrons arranged 2, 8 — the same stable arrangement as neon.
misconception: 2, 8, 1 is the neutral atom; a positive ion has LOST electrons.
hints: How many electrons does Na⁺ have?

subject: Chemistry
q: An aluminium atom has mass number 27 and atomic number 13. How many neutrons does it have?
explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 27 − 13 = 14.
hints: Mass number = protons + neutrons.

subject: Chemistry
q: Natural chlorine is about 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. What is its average atomic mass?
explanation: Average = 0.75 × 35 + 0.25 × 37 = 26.25 + 9.25 = 35.5 u. It is closer to 35 because chlorine-35 is three times as abundant.
misconception: 36 u is the simple average, which ignores the abundances.
hints: Weight each isotope’s mass by its abundance.

subject: Chemistry
q: An element has only two isotopes, of mass 10 u and 11 u, and an average atomic mass of 10.8 u. What percentage of its atoms are the lighter isotope?
explanation: Let x be the fraction of mass-10 atoms: 10x + 11(1 − x) = 10.8 → 11 − x = 10.8 → x = 0.2, i.e. 20%. Sense check: the average (10.8) is much closer to 11, so the heavier isotope must dominate. (This is boron.)
misconception: 80% is the abundance of the heavier isotope — check which side the average lies on.
hints: Let the fraction of mass-10 atoms be x; the rest are mass 11.
Is 10.8 closer to 10 or to 11? Which isotope is more common?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which pair of atoms are isobars?
explanation: Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers: argon-40 (Z = 18) and calcium-40 (Z = 20). C-12/C-14 and ¹H/²H are isotopes (same Z, different A).
misconception: Isotopes = same element (same Z); isobars = same mass number (same A).
hints: Isobars share the same mass number.

subject: Chemistry
q:
Assertion (A): Isotopes of an element have almost identical chemical properties.
Reason (R): Chemical properties depend mainly on the number and arrangement of electrons, which is the same for isotopes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
explanation: Isotopes differ only in the number of neutrons. They have the same number of protons and therefore the same electron arrangement, and electrons — especially valence electrons — govern chemical behaviour. R correctly explains A.
misconception: Neutrons change the mass (and nuclear stability), not the chemistry.
hints: What differs between isotopes?

subject: Chemistry
q: The M shell can hold up to 18 electrons, yet potassium (Z = 19) has the configuration 2, 8, 8, 1 rather than 2, 8, 9. Why?
options: The N shell fills before the M shell in every atom.
The M shell can only hold 8 electrons.
The outermost shell of an atom cannot hold more than 8 electrons.
explanation: In the Bohr–Bury scheme taught in Class IX, the outermost shell can hold at most 8 electrons. Putting 9 in the M shell would make it an outermost shell with 9, so the 19th electron goes into the N shell. (The deeper reason — energy levels of sub-shells — is studied in higher classes.)
misconception: The M shell can hold 18, but not while it is the outermost shell.
hints: What is the maximum number of electrons allowed in the OUTERMOST shell?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which correctly describes a neutron?
options: Positive charge, mass about equal to a proton
No charge, mass about equal to a proton
explanation: Neutrons, discovered by James Chadwick in 1932, are neutral particles in the nucleus with a mass very slightly greater than a proton’s (≈ 1 u).
misconception: Neutral does not mean massless.
hints: Neutrons are found in the nucleus with protons.

subject: Chemistry
q: Suppose Thomson’s “plum-pudding” model (positive charge spread evenly through the atom, electrons embedded in it) had been correct. What would Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment have shown?
options: No alpha particles passing through at all
Nearly all alpha particles passing through with only small deflections and none bouncing back
Most alpha particles bouncing straight back
Alpha particles being absorbed and turned into gold
explanation: With positive charge spread thinly, no region of the atom would have a strong enough concentrated charge to turn back a fast, heavy alpha particle — only slight deflections would occur. The observed rare large deflections (about 1 in 20,000 bounced back) proved that the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
misconception: Spreading the same charge over a bigger volume makes the repulsion at any point much weaker.
hints: Where is the positive charge in Thomson’s model — concentrated or spread out?
Can a thinly spread charge exert a strong force on a fast, heavy particle?

subject: Chemistry
q: Which of these is a compound?
explanation: Water (H₂O) has hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio with new properties. Air and sea water are mixtures; brass is an alloy of copper and zinc — a mixture whose composition can vary.
misconception: Alloys look uniform, but they are mixtures, not compounds.
hints: Which substance has a fixed chemical formula?

subject: Chemistry
q: How can camphor be separated from a mixture of camphor and common salt?
explanation: Camphor sublimes (turns directly to vapour on gentle heating) and re-solidifies on a cool surface, while salt does not. Both are soluble-ish solids, so filtration alone would not work.
hints: Which of the two substances changes from solid directly to vapour?

subject: Chemistry
q: A drop of black marker ink on filter paper is dipped in water. After some time the spot spreads into separate blue, yellow and red bands. What can you conclude?
options: The ink is a mixture of dyes that travel at different rates.
Water reacts with the ink to make new coloured compounds.
The ink is a pure compound that decomposes.
explanation: This is paper chromatography. Each dye has a different solubility in the solvent and attraction to the paper, so they move different distances and separate. A pure substance gives a single spot.
misconception: No chemical reaction occurs — chromatography is a physical separation.
hints: What would a pure substance look like on the paper?

subject: Chemistry
q: 20 g of salt is dissolved in 180 g of water. What is the concentration of the solution as a mass-by-mass percentage?
explanation: Mass % = mass of solute ÷ mass of SOLUTION × 100 = 20 ÷ (20 + 180) × 100 = 20/200 × 100 = 10%.
misconception: 11.1% divides by the mass of the solvent (180 g) instead of the whole solution (200 g).
hints: Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.

subject: Chemistry
q: Which technique is used in dairies to separate cream from milk?
explanation: Spinning milk at high speed in a centrifuge forces the denser parts outward and the lighter fat (cream) collects near the centre, where it is drawn off. The same principle is used to separate blood cells from plasma.
hints: Cream is less dense than the rest of milk.

subject: Chemistry
q: A narrow torch beam is shone through four liquids. In which will the path of the beam be clearly visible from the side?
explanation: Milk is a colloid: its fat and protein particles are big enough to scatter light (the Tyndall effect), making the beam visible. In true solutions (salt, sugar, copper sulphate) the particles are too small to scatter light noticeably.
misconception: A coloured solution (copper sulphate) is still a true solution — colour is not the same as scattering.
hints: Which liquid is a colloid?

subject: Chemistry
